bp: This paper is about phishing before it reaches the victim's inbox. A phishing attack looks, from the outside, like a fake login page, a deceptive email, and stolen credentials. But before that visible moment, attackers need supplies: page templates, mail servers, stolen account lists, instructions, buyers, sellers, and people who know which services are worth imitating. The paper treats Deep and Dark Web forums as a marketplace and workshop where that supply chain leaves written traces. Instead of only studying attacks after damage is reported, it asks what can be learned by watching how phishing campaigns are assembled. The study collects 394,034 forum posts from 13 forums between 2013 and 2025, identifies 70,055 phishing-related posts, and extracts what components are discussed, what services are targeted, and who authors those components. The goal is practical: give defenders earlier visibility into attack materials and market shifts.
wh: The hard part is that phishing is not one object. It is a moving ecosystem made from many small pieces that change over time. A credential list, a phishing kit, a fake page, an SMTP server, and a targeted brand are different things, but together they describe attack readiness. Forum posts are also messy evidence. Sellers advertise, buyers ask questions, people reuse names, posts repeat, and the same component can appear in different wording. Looking only at confirmed attacks misses the upstream market where tools are traded before deployment. Looking only at forum keyword counts misses the structure of the attack: which component belongs to which stage, which service is being imitated, and whether a post describes supply, demand, or technique sharing. The time span adds another difficulty. A pattern that matters in 2013 may mean something different in 2025 as services, attacker tools, and prices change.
naive: A smart beginner might collect known phishing URLs or breach reports and count which brands appear most often. That would be useful, but it would see the crime after the machinery has already run. Another simple attempt would be to search dark-web forum posts for words like phishing, PayPal, or credentials, then plot those counts over time. That fails because counts alone do not say what attackers are building. A post mentioning Netflix could be selling a ready-made page, asking for stolen logins, discussing mail delivery, or naming a target in passing. Without extracting components and stages, the analysis cannot distinguish an emerging supply-chain change from loose chatter.
ap: The core move is to turn unstructured forum conversation into a structured map of phishing production. The paper first separates phishing-related posts from a much larger forum archive. Then it uses a large language model, meaning a text model trained to read and generate language, as an extraction tool for recurring facts: attack components such as credentials, phishing pages, kits, and SMTP servers; targeted services such as PayPal or Netflix; and component authors. Those extracted facts are not left as a bag of labels. They are mapped into a seven-stage attack scenario built from empirical case studies, so each item is placed inside an attack process. Once posts become dated, staged, and typed records, the authors can study how component availability, target-service distribution, post types, active contributors, and prices evolve across twelve years.
mech: The mechanism starts with a dated archive: 394,034 posts, 343,334 of them unique, from 13 Deep and Dark Web forums between 2013 and 2025. The first transformation is filtering. The study identifies 70,055 posts as phishing-related, reducing a broad underground-forum collection to the portion relevant to phishing supply and knowledge exchange. The second transformation is extraction. A language model reads the selected posts and pulls out structured pieces of information that defenders can compare: what component is being discussed, what service is targeted, and who is associated with the component. The third transformation is organization by attack stage. The extracted pieces are mapped to a seven-stage attack scenario, which turns scattered posts into evidence about where each item fits in the life of an attack. The fourth step is measurement over time. Because every post has a forum source and date, the paper can count and compare component availability, changes in target services, evolution of post types, yearly active contributors, and component prices. The output is not a detector for one incoming email. It is a longitudinal picture of the underground market that shows how phishing infrastructure and methods have shifted over more than a decade.
math: Several mathematical ideas sit underneath the study. The first is classification: deciding whether each forum post belongs in the phishing pile. In plain terms, classification means learning or applying a rule that separates one kind of text from another when the boundary is not obvious from a single word. The second is information extraction: turning sentences into fields. This is a structured reading problem, where the system must map many ways of saying the same thing into comparable records such as component, target service, author, and price. The third is time-series counting, which means placing comparable events on a calendar and watching their frequency change. A rise in phishing-kit availability or a shift in named targets matters only if the counting method keeps the meaning of each item stable enough across years. The fourth idea is taxonomy, or sorting observations into a staged model of an attack. That staged model is a simplifying map: it loses some detail from individual conversations, but it makes thousands of posts comparable. The main tradeoff is scale versus certainty. A language model can read far more posts than human analysts, but its extracted fields must be trusted only to the extent that the post language and validation support them.
dots: This paper connects security, text mining, market measurement, and longitudinal web analysis. Like misinformation and trust studies, it treats online communities as places where harmful behavior is prepared, normalized, and coordinated before outsiders see the full result. Like fraud and anomaly work, it tries to move from isolated incidents to patterns in infrastructure. Like retrieval and extraction papers, it must turn messy text into structured facts that can be searched, counted, and compared. The difference is the object being organized: not users and products, but attacker resources and campaign ingredients. Its closest conceptual neighbors are papers that study adversarial behavior, evolving online ecosystems, and language-model-assisted analysis of large document collections. The shared problem is that the useful signal is buried in informal text, spread across many sources, and meaningful only when connected across time.
ww: The approach works better than post-attack analysis because it observes the preparation layer. If phishing campaigns require components, then conversations about buying, selling, authoring, and using those components are early evidence of capability. A fake page does not appear from nowhere; someone offers it, requests it, modifies it, prices it, or pairs it with delivery infrastructure. By extracting component types and mapping them to attack stages, the study converts noisy forum talk into a supply-chain view. That matters because defenders do not only need to know which emails were sent last week. They need to know which tools are becoming easy to obtain, which services attackers currently discuss, and which contributors repeatedly shape the market. The twelve-year span also separates short bursts from durable changes. A one-month spike may be noise; a repeated rise in a component class or target service across years suggests a real shift in attacker practice.
po: The payoff is earlier and broader visibility into phishing than post-attack datasets can provide. The paper offers a macro-level view of the attacker side of the ecosystem: 70,055 phishing-related posts, extracted components, target services, component authors, post-type changes, active contributors, and pricing dynamics across 2013 to 2025. That can help defenders prioritize monitoring, detection, and prevention around the parts of the supply chain that are becoming easier to buy or more often discussed. The contribution is not just another list of phishing incidents; it is a structured account of how phishing infrastructure and markets have evolved.
limits: The claims depend on the forums being a useful window into the phishing market. If important activity moved to private chats, closed groups, or platforms outside the 13 forums, the picture may miss parts of the ecosystem. The language-model extraction also has limits: forum slang, deception, duplicate posts, and ambiguous seller claims can lead to wrong or incomplete fields. Mapping posts to seven attack stages makes analysis possible, but real campaigns may not follow that order cleanly. The abstract reports trends and market structure, not proof that a specific forum discussion caused a specific attack wave.
